Ubuntu 26.04: Reliable Desktop Linux
recent_posts.summary: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon) has been released, featuring Linux kernel 7.0, GNOME 50 with Wayland-only support, hardware-backed TPM 2.0 disk encryption, improved Nvidia driver setup, and several new apps rewritten in Rust (Papers PDF viewer, Showtime video player, Lupe image viewer). System requirements now list 6 GB RAM (up from 4 GB). Notable changes include a new security center app, sudo-rs replacing sudo, a text size slider for accessibility, and Pipewire distributed as a snap package. The video also addresses common criticisms of Ubuntu around Canonical's commercial involvement and the snap packaging system.

recent_posts.title: RISC-V 2026 Update
recent_posts.summary: A 2026 annual review of the RISC-V open ISA ecosystem covering major developments over the past year. Key highlights include Meta's acquisition of Rivos and Qualcomm's acquisition of Ventana Microsystems, RISC-V International's first annual report and ISO PAS recognition, and the ratification of the RVA23 profile enabling binary-compatible application processors. Growing adoption spans automotive (software-defined vehicles), AI accelerators (Meta MTIA, Google Coral NPU, SiFive), and data center servers. New hardware like the SpacemiT K3 SoC and Milk-V Jupiter 2 board are arriving, while Linux distros including Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, RHEL, and Debian 13 are adding RISC-V support. Market predictions suggest RISC-V will reach 33.7% penetration by 2031 with over 35 billion shipped SoCs containing a RISC-V core.

recent_posts.title: Microsoft Office alternatives for Linux compared
recent_posts.summary: A practical comparison of four Microsoft Office alternatives for Linux: LibreOffice, FreeOffice/SoftMaker Office, OnlyOffice, and WPS Office. The primary evaluation criterion is document fidelity — how accurately each suite renders Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files compared to the originals. Results show that no Linux alternative achieves perfect fidelity with .docx files, though spreadsheet and presentation compatibility is generally better. LibreOffice and SoftMaker Office are recommended as the best overall options, with the author personally planning to switch to SoftMaker Office when Windows 10 support ends.

recent_posts.title: Long-Term Data Storage for Home Users
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive overview of long-term data storage options for home users, covering hard drives, SSDs, USB drives, optical media, and cloud storage. Explains the difference between data backup and archiving, provides expected data retention periods for each media type, and offers practical guidance on refresh schedules. Key takeaways include: hard drives retain data ~5 years (refresh every 3 years), SSDs are not ideal for cold storage due to electron leakage, archival-grade optical discs can last 50+ years, and cloud storage offloads preservation responsibility but can be costly at scale. Recommends keeping at least two copies with one offsite, and applying the 3-2-1 backup rule where feasible.

recent_posts.title: Lightweight Linux for Older Computers
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide to running lightweight Linux distributions on older hardware, categorized into three tiers: 64-bit systems with 4GB+ RAM, 64-bit systems with less than 4GB RAM, and 32-bit processors. Tests include Ubuntu, Lubuntu, MX Linux, Linux Lite, Q4OS, and AntiX across machines ranging from a 12-year-old Intel Core i3 to an 18-year-old Atom-based netbook. Memory usage benchmarks are provided for each distro, and Q4OS with the Trinity desktop stands out for very low-spec hardware. The guide also notes that 32-bit Linux support is declining, with Debian 13 dropping 32-bit support entirely.

recent_posts.title: Linux Age Verification: FOSS in the Brave New World
recent_posts.summary: New age verification laws in California, Brazil, and other jurisdictions are requiring operating system providers to collect user age data and provide age bracket signals to applications via API. This creates significant practical and philosophical challenges for Linux distros, which lack centralized governance, commercial backing, and existing parental control infrastructure. Commercial Linux providers like Canonical, Red Hat, and System 76 will likely need to comply, while community distros may opt for disclaimers or non-compliance. A key concern is that non-compliant distros may have their users treated as under-13 by default, delivering a degraded internet experience. The author warns this legislation may be just the beginning, with future laws potentially requiring full ID-based age verification at OS install time, fundamentally conflicting with Linux's FOSS and privacy principles.

recent_posts.title: Pikimov: Free Motion Graphics & Video Editing Web App
recent_posts.summary: Pikimov (formerly Pikmi Move) is a free browser-based motion graphics and video compositing tool inspired by Adobe After Effects. It runs entirely locally with no cloud uploads and works on Linux, Windows, and macOS via Chrome/Edge. The walkthrough covers layer-based 2D compositing with keyframe animation, text masking, motion tracking, chroma keying combined with AI-based background removal, and a classic video editor with transitions and effects. While not as feature-rich as After Effects, it handles standard motion graphics tasks well and is especially valuable for Linux users who lack layer-based compositing alternatives.

recent_posts.title: Consumer SBCs in 2026
recent_posts.summary: A retrospective look at the consumer single board computer (SBC) market in 2025-2026, examining why SBCs are becoming less popular with home users. Key factors include rising prices making mini PCs more competitive, the industry's AI focus not aligning with hobbyist needs, and the loss of the 'pioneering' excitement that once made ARM SBCs novel. Raspberry Pi sold 7.6 million units in 2025 but ~70% went to businesses. The hobbyist frontier has shifted toward Linux on traditional hardware, generative AI experimentation, and RISC-V boards. The author also outlines a shift in their own content strategy toward lower-cost maker-focused SBCs and microcontrollers.

recent_posts.title: DIY Mini-ITX Case
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on build log of a scratch-built Mini-ITX PC case made from 2mm ABS plastic sheet. The builder covers material selection (ABS sheet, liquid poly adhesive, M3 standoffs), cutting and assembly techniques, power supply choice (TFX Gamemax GT450G), front panel components (USB 3 ports, power switch with LED), cooling strategy, and finishing with filler, sanding, and spray paint. The final case measures 281×193×94mm (5.1L volume) and cost roughly £60 excluding the PSU. Temperature tests under Linux Mint showed idle temps around 30°C and a peak of 61°C under a 30-minute Blender render, confirming adequate passive and PSU-driven airflow.
